title: Moses Looks Back
subtitle: Deuteronomy 1 to 4, Berean Standard Bible
description: Moses retells the journey for the children who did not live it, from Horeb and the spies to the sentence, the long bypass, and his own refused plea to cross the Jordan.
paragraphs: "These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan"

That is the book's own first line, and it is a title as much as a sentence. What follows is not a new journey. It is a speech, the longest goodbye in the Bible, given by a man of 120 who knows the land in front of his audience is closed to him.
"In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses proclaimed to the Israelites all that the LORD had commanded him concerning them."

The people listening were not, most of them, the people who had lived the story. Their parents had come out of Egypt, stood at Sinai, refused the land, and died in the wilderness over forty years. The crowd on the plains of Moab was their children, grown, armed, counted, and facing the Jordan. Egypt was a story their mothers told. Sinai was a mountain they had never seen. So before Moses gave them a single law, he gave them their own history, told by the only man standing who had been an adult for all of it.
He started with the distance.

It is an eleven day journey from Horeb, the mountain of God, to Kadesh Barnea, on the border of the land. Eleven days. The people Moses addressed had spent forty years covering it, and he did not let that arithmetic sit in the background of the speech. It was the speech's whole point.

At Horeb, God had said to them: you have stayed at this mountain long enough. Break camp and advance into the hill country of the Amorites and all their neighbors, the whole land of Canaan spread out in the command, the Arabah, the hills, the lowland, the Negev, the coast, the great river Euphrates.
"See, I have placed the land before you. Enter and possess the land that the LORD swore He would give to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants after them."

But a nation of that size could not be judged by one man, and Moses told them how the burden had been shared before the march began. The LORD your God has multiplied you, he said, until you are as numerous as the stars in the sky. How can I bear your burdens and your disputes by myself? So the tribes chose wise, understanding, respected men, and Moses set them as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and charged their judges with the rule he now repeated for their children to hear.
"Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike. Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God. And bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it."

Then Moses came to the event the whole speech turns on, and he told it with an angle the children in front of him may never have heard stated plainly. In Numbers, the sending of the spies begins with God's command to Moses. In Moses' own retelling, it begins with the people.
"Then all of you approached me and said," Moses recalled, "Let us send men ahead of us to search out the land and bring us word of what route to follow and which cities to enter."

The idea seemed good to Moses, he said, and he took twelve men, one from each tribe. They went up into the hill country, came to the valley of Eshcol, took some of the fruit of the land in their hands, and brought it down with the report the new generation had grown up hearing: it is a good land the LORD our God is giving us. The grapes were real. So was everything that happened next.
"But you were unwilling to go up; you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God."

"You grumbled in your tents and said," Moses told them: "Because the LORD hates us, He has brought us out of the land of Egypt to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be annihilated." That was the charge their parents had made in their tents: not fear of giants, but hatred, laid on the God who had carried them.

Moses told them what he had said to their parents on that night, and part of it is as tender as anything in the five books. Do not be terrified, do not be afraid of them. The LORD your God, who goes before you, will fight for you, just as He did for you in Egypt before your very eyes.
"And in the wilderness, where the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way by which you traveled until you reached this place."

They would not trust Him, not even then, not with Egypt behind them and the evidence in their own memories. So the LORD heard the sound of their words and swore the oath their children were now living inside: not one of the men of this evil generation shall see the good land I swore to give your fathers, except Caleb son of Jephunneh, who followed the LORD wholeheartedly, and Joshua son of Nun, standing beside Moses now, who would lead the children in.

And then Moses said the sentence his audience most needed to hear him say, because it closed the question of why the old man speaking would not be crossing the river with them. He said it his way, and the book leaves it standing in his words.

Moses put his own case in one sentence, and he put it in the form he would use again in this book: "The LORD was also angry with me on your account, and He said," and then the sentence itself, "Not even you shall enter the land."

Numbers tells the waters of Meribah from the narrator's side, Moses striking the rock he was told to speak to, and the sentence falling on Moses and Aaron there. Deuteronomy is Moses' own account of his case, given in his own farewell, and he lays his exclusion at the door of the people's rebellion, here and twice more in the book. The two records are not reconciled for the reader, because the text does not reconcile them. What is certain in both is the outcome: Moses would see the land. Moses would not enter it.

The retelling did not stop at the sentence. Moses told them how their parents had tried to reverse it the next morning, going up into the hill country against the word, after being told the LORD was not with them.
"But the LORD said to me," Moses recalled, "Tell them not to go up and fight, for I am not with you to keep you from defeat by your enemies." They had the warning in full before they climbed.

They went anyway, and the Amorites came out like a swarm of bees and chased them as far as Hormah. The people stayed at Kadesh many days. Then began the long detour that ate the rest of the generation, and Moses walked his listeners through its rules, because the rules of the detour were themselves a lesson about land and promise. God had given Mount Seir to Esau's descendants and would not let Israel take a foot of it. He had given Ar to the descendants of Lot, the Moabites, and later the Ammonites their land, and Israel was to pass by in peace, buying food with silver and water with silver, disturbing nothing. The lands east of the promised land already had owners, and their titles came from the same God. Giants had lived in those countries before, the Emim in Moab, the Zamzummim in Ammon, tall peoples the ancients counted alongside the Anakim, and God had dispossessed them for Lot's children the way He was about to dispossess nations for Israel. The gift to Israel was not the only gift on the map.
Through all of it, Moses said, God had kept them.

"Indeed, the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He has watched over your journey through this vast wilderness. The LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing."

"The time we spent traveling from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed over the Brook of Zered was thirty-eight years, until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them."

Thirty-eight years between one brook and the sentence's end. The hand of the LORD was against that generation until it had perished from the camp, and only when the last of the counted men had died did the road turn north again, toward kings who would fight.

Moses retold Sihon briefly, the way a man summarizes a battle his audience has already heard sung. Israel had sent messengers with words of peace, asking the highway, offering to buy food and water. Sihon refused, because the LORD had hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, in order to deliver him into Israel's hand, and he marched out to Jahaz and lost everything: his cities taken, his people devoted to destruction, the livestock and plunder kept. God's word to Moses at the start of that campaign is the line Moses chose to repeat.
"See, I have begun to deliver Sihon and his land over to you. Now begin to conquer and possess his land."
"From Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the valley, even as far as Gilead, not one city had walls too high for us. The LORD our God gave us all of them."

Og of Bashan followed: sixty cities taken, the whole region of Argob, fortified cities with high walls, gates, and bars, and no survivor, while the cities without walls and the livestock were taken as plunder. Moses had given the conquered land to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, with the oath their fathers swore and the new generation had heard rehearsed in Numbers: cross armed ahead of your brothers. Then he had charged Joshua in their hearing, and he repeated the charge now, in front of the son's generation. Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So the LORD will do to all the kingdoms over there. Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you.
Then the farewell turned personal, and Moses let them hear the one prayer of his that God refused.

"At that time I also pleaded with the LORD," he said. "O Lord GOD, You have begun to show Your greatness and power to Your servant. For what god in heaven or on earth can perform such works and mighty acts as Yours?" And then the request itself: "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan," Moses begged, "that pleasant hill country as well as Lebanon!"

"But the LORD was angry with me on account of you, and He would not listen to me." Then came the refusal, in words that end all argument: "That is enough," the LORD said to me. "Do not speak to Me again about this matter." The matter was closed, by name.
"Go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west and north and south and east. See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan."
"But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him, for he will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit the land that you will see."

The man who had spent forty years successfully arguing God out of destroying Israel could not argue his own sentence down by one river's width. God gave him the mountain view instead, and a successor to strengthen, and silence on the subject from then on.

Chapter 4 turns the history into its lesson, and it is the first sermon proper of the book. Now, Israel, hear the statutes and ordinances I am teaching you. Do not add to them. Do not subtract from them.
"You must not add to or subtract from what I command you, so that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you."

Moses pointed their memory at the most recent proof. Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal Peor: every man who followed Baal of Peor, the LORD destroyed from among you, but you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today. The children listening were the survivors of that plague's generation, and some of them had been there. Then he set the keeping of the law in front of the nations watching: keep the statutes, for this is your wisdom and understanding in the sight of the peoples, who will say, surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people. What other great nation has God so near, or statutes as righteous as this whole law?
Then the guard at the center of it.

"Only be on your guard and diligently watch yourselves, so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen, and so that they do not slip from your heart as long as you live. Teach them to your children and grandchildren."

Remember the day you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, Moses said, reaching back past the children's births to the mountain their parents had trembled at, when God had gathered the people to hear His words so that they would learn to fear Him and teach their children. They had heard a voice out of the fire and seen no form. That formlessness became the sermon's hammer. Because you saw no form when the LORD spoke at Horeb, watch yourselves carefully: do not act corruptly by making an idol in any likeness, male or female, animal, bird, crawler, or fish, and do not be drawn to worship the sun, the moon, and the stars, the host of heaven allotted to all the peoples under heaven. Egypt's gods had shapes. The God who spoke from the fire had a voice and no shape, and the children were to keep Him that way in their minds.
"For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God."

And then Moses did something no summary of the sermon should skip, because it is the first time in the five books that the whole future is laid out in one paragraph. If, after settling in the land and growing old there, they corrupted themselves with images and did evil, heaven and earth would witness against them, and they would perish quickly from the land and be scattered among the peoples, few in number, serving gods of wood and stone that neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell. All of it, Moses said in advance: the conquest, the corruption, the exile, and then the turn.
"But if from there you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul."
"When you are in distress and all these things have happened to you, then in later days you will return to the LORD your God and listen to His voice."
"For the LORD your God is a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers, which He swore to them by oath."

The sermon closed where the whole book aims. Ask about the days of old, Moses said, since God created man on the earth, from one end of heaven to the other: has anything this great ever happened, or has anything like it been heard of? Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking from the fire and lived? Has God ever taken a nation for Himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, signs, wonders, war, a mighty hand and an outstretched arm?
"You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him."
"Know therefore this day and take to heart that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other."

Moses set apart three cities east of the Jordan for the manslayer to flee to, Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan, the other side of the refuge system Numbers had built. And the narrator closes the first address with a sentence that sets the stage for the second: this is the law that Moses set before the Israelites, the testimonies, statutes, and ordinances he spoke when they came out of Egypt, in the land they had already taken, at the edge of the land they had not.
The old man had covered forty years in one speech, and he had not yet opened the law itself. That was next, and he began it the only place it could begin: back at the mountain, with the ten words.

title: Hear, O Israel
subtitle: Deuteronomy 5 to 11, Berean Standard Bible
description: The commandments are given again, the Shema is taught, and Moses warns against forgetting when the houses are full, retelling the golden calf from his side of the mountain.
paragraphs: Moses summoned all Israel and began the second address where the first one had pointed: back at the mountain.
"Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day. Learn them and observe them carefully."

The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb, he told them, and he was careful about the word us. Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, with all of us who are alive here today. The parents who had stood at the foot of that mountain and heard the voice out of the fire were dead in the wilderness, every one of them but Caleb and Joshua. The crowd on the plains was their children, and Moses opened the law by handing them their parents' mountain as their own. Face to face, he said, the LORD spoke with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire. I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain.

Then he read the ten words again, the same ten Israel had heard in Exodus, and a first-time reader working through the books in order can hear the seams where the second giving differs from the first.
"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery."

You shall have no other gods before Me. You shall not make an idol in any form, or bow down to them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments. You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain. Observe the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet.

The Sabbath is where the difference lives, and Moses left it where any listener could find it. In Exodus, God rested on the seventh day of creation, and that was the reason given at Sinai for Israel's rest. Here the commandment carries a second reason, an Egyptian one.

"Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day."

Rest, in the second telling, is not only God imitated. It is slavery remembered. The man who worked seven days under Pharaoh because no one would let him stop now stops, and lets his servants and his animals stop, because his God broke the hand that held the whip. The law reads differently when the reason is a memory instead of a doctrine, and Moses clearly meant his listeners, most of whom had been born free in the wilderness, to feel the weight of a slavery they had inherited as a story rather than a scar.

Moses retold the terror of that day too: the mountain burning, the voice, the people's plea that he go near and listen for them, because this great fire will consume us and we will die if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer. And God's answer to the plea, which Moses had never had reason to repeat until now, is one of the most human lines God speaks in the five books.
"If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always, so that it might be well with them and with their children forever."

Then chapter 6, the sermon's core, the passage Israel would carry on its doorposts and its lips into every generation after. It opens with the confession that would outlive the nation, the temple, and the language it was written in.
"Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One."
"And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength."
"These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts."
"And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up."

Bind them as a sign on your hand, Moses said, let them be as frontlets between your eyes, write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates. The commandments were not given as scrolls to be archived. They were given as talk at the table, talk on the road, the last words at night and the first in the morning, words on the doors a child passes through twenty times a day. The second generation listening had been raised in tents by parents under a death sentence, and Moses was telling them how the faith survives a generation: not by monument, but by repetition, until a child who never saw the sea split can say the words as his own.

And immediately, the warning that runs under this whole section like groundwater. When the LORD brings you into the land, a land with great and splendid cities you did not build, houses full of good things you did not fill them with, wells you did not dig, vineyards and olive groves you did not plant, and when you eat and are satisfied, then:
"Be careful not to forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery."
"Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only, and take your oaths in His name."

Do not follow other gods, the gods of the peoples around you. Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah. Tell your son, when he asks in time to come what these testimonies mean, the whole story in one breath, the way Moses framed it for them: we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt, and the LORD brought us out with a mighty hand, and He gave us this land, and He commanded these statutes for our good, to preserve us alive. Obedience, in Moses' telling, is not a tax. It is the shape of the rescue, continued.
Chapter 7 told them why they, of all peoples, were standing there. It was not their size.
"The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples."
"But because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers, He brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt."
"Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments."

They were to break down the altars of the land's peoples, smash their sacred stones, burn their idols, make no covenant and show no pity, because the snare was real: intermarriage would turn their children after other gods, and the anger of the LORD would destroy them quickly. You are a people holy to the LORD your God, Moses said, His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth. And he promised the other side of the arrangement in plain terms: God would keep the loving devotion, bless the fruit of womb and ground, remove sickness, and drive the nations out little by little, so the wild animals would not multiply against Israel in the empty land. Even the conquest, in the sermon, runs on God's timing rather than Israel's strength.
Chapter 8 reached back to the forty years and told the children what the wilderness had been for. It had been a test, and the test had a grader's purpose.

"Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments."

"He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD."
"Your clothing did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years."

As a man disciplines his son, Moses said, the LORD your God disciplined you. And the land ahead of them was described in the sermon's warmest passage: a good land, brooks of water, fountains and springs flowing in valleys and hills, wheat and barley, vines, fig trees, pomegranates, olive oil and honey, a land where bread would not be scarce and iron could be dug from the hills and copper from the mountains. Eat, be satisfied, bless the LORD. And there the warning returns, sharper for being set in plenty: when your herds multiply and your silver and gold increase and your heart is lifted up, you will forget. There is a sentence people start saying in a full house that no one says in a tent.
"You might say in your heart" the warning runs, and the sentence it pictures is this: "The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me." Wealth, in the saying, has a single author.
"But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day."

If you ever forget, Moses said, and walk after other gods, I testify against you today that you will surely perish, like the nations the LORD destroys before you. The sermon has no version of events where the gifts survive the forgetting of the Giver.

Then Moses made the point the whole generation most needed to hear, in the sermon and probably in the book, and he made it three times so it could not be missed. When the nations fell before them, they were not to say the sentence already forming in human hearts.

"When the LORD your God has driven them out before you, do not say in your heart," the warning runs, and the sentence it forbids is this: "Because of my righteousness the LORD has brought me in to possess this land." Then Moses answers it himself: "Rather, the LORD is driving out these nations before you because of their wickedness."
"It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land."
"Understand, then, that it is not because of your righteousness that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people."

And to prove the charge, Moses walked them through their parents' record, and his own, at the mountain. Remember, do not forget, how you provoked the LORD in the wilderness. From the day you left Egypt until you arrived here, you have been rebellious. At Horeb itself, while Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights without bread or water, receiving the tablets of the covenant, the people below had already built the calf. Their own history's holiest month is the indictment.

"When I went up on the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I ate no bread and drank no water."
"And at the end of forty days and forty nights, the LORD gave me the two stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant."
"And I saw how you had sinned against the LORD your God; you had made for yourselves a molten calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you."

He took the two tablets in his two hands, Moses said, and threw them down and broke them before their eyes, the way Exodus records. Then, what Exodus records only in outline, Moses laid out in detail: he fell down before the LORD for forty days and forty nights a second time, eating no bread and drinking no water, because of the sin they had committed, while the LORD said He would destroy them and blot out their name. He feared the anger and the wrath, he said plainly. And he prayed for Aaron too, whom the LORD was angry enough to destroy. He took the calf, burned it, ground it to powder as fine as dust, and threw the dust into the brook that ran down the mountain. Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, Kadesh Barnea: the list of provocations runs through the retelling like place names on a road map of rebellion, ending at Kadesh, where the parents had refused the land and sent Moses back with the report that cost forty years.
His prayer from those forty days is preserved, and it is the same shape as his prayer at the sea of reeds in reverse: not spare me, but spare them.
"O Lord GOD, do not destroy Your people, Your inheritance, whom You redeemed through Your greatness and brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand."
"Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Overlook the stubbornness of this people and the wickedness of their sin."

The argument he made to God then is the argument he was now making to Israel: they are Your people. What the nations would say if Egypt's God destroyed His own rescued people in the wilderness runs through the plea to the end.
"But they are Your people, Your inheritance, whom You brought out by Your great power and outstretched arm."
Chapter 10 answers the broken tablets. At that time, God told Moses to chisel two stone tablets like the first, come up the mountain, and make an ark of wood.
"Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, come up to Me on the mountain, and make an ark of wood."
"And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke; and you are to place them in the ark."

Moses made the ark of acacia wood, chiseled the tablets, went up with them in his hand, and God wrote on them the words of the first tablets, the ten commandments proclaimed at the assembly. He came down and placed them in the ark.
"And I went back down the mountain and placed the tablets in the ark I had made, as the LORD had commanded me; and there they have remained."

The broken covenant ends up carried in a box, whole again, at the center of the camp. Aaron died on the road after that, at Moserah, and Eleazar his son took his place, and the tribe of Levi was set apart to carry the ark and stand before the LORD and bless in His name, receiving no land inheritance because the LORD is their inheritance. It is the order Israel had lived under for forty years, retold in a paragraph as Moses prepares them to live under it in a land of farms instead of a moving camp.
Then the sermon's summary, the whole second address folded into one question and answer.

"And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul,"
"And to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you this day for your own good?"

Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the highest heaven, the earth and all that is in it. Yet He set His affection on your fathers, loved them, and chose their descendants. So the command that follows is aimed at the organ every failure in the story has come from.
"Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more."
"For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe."
"He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing."
Love the foreigner, Moses added, because you were foreigners in Egypt. Swear by His name. He is your praise and your God, who did the great and awesome wonders your eyes have seen.
"Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars in the sky."

Chapter 11 binds the section shut with the choice in its first form. Love the LORD and keep His charge always, so you will have the strength to go in and possess the land. The land ahead is not Egypt: it does not drink from a river at your foot, it drinks rain from heaven, and a land the LORD your God cares for, His eyes always on it, from the beginning of the year to the end. If you carefully obey, He will give the rains in season, the autumn and the spring rains, and you will gather grain, new wine, and oil, and eat and be satisfied. Take heed that your hearts are not deceived and you turn aside to other gods, because then the rains stop and the good land gives up its people quickly.
The words are to be fixed and taught the same way chapter 6 commanded, and then the geography of the rest of the book is set down in a single sentence.
"See, today I am setting before you a blessing and a curse"
"A blessing if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you today,"
"But a curse if you disobey the commandments of the LORD your God and turn aside from the path I command you today by following other gods, which you have not known."

When the LORD brings you into the land, Moses said, the blessing is to be proclaimed on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal, two mountains across from each other beyond the Jordan, waiting already in the landscape for the ceremony of chapter 27. The choice will one day be read aloud off two hillsides with the whole nation answering. Here, at the end of his second address, Moses only names it.

The law itself, the statutes for courts and fields and tables, was next. But the order matters, and Moses kept it: first the mountain, first the one God and the wholehearted love, first the warning about full houses. Rules for a settled life would land differently on people who had been told, three ways, that the life was a gift.

title: One Altar, and Laws for Settled Life
subtitle: Deuteronomy 12 to 16, Berean Standard Bible
description: Worship gathers to one chosen place, false prophets are tested, and the tithe, the seventh-year release, and the three feasts order the life of a settled people.
paragraphs: The second address had begun at the mountain. Now Moses turned from the mountain to the land itself, to towns his hearers did not yet own, gates they had never walked through, fields they had never planted. Almost everything in these chapters is future tense. He was describing a settled life to a camp, and the first statute he gave them was about where God would be worshiped.

"Destroy completely all the places where the nations you are dispossessing have served their gods". Their worship was everywhere, he said, on the high mountains, on the hills, under every green tree. Israel was to tear down the altars, smash the sacred pillars, burn the Asherah poles, cut down the idols, and wipe out the very names of those gods from every place. "You shall not worship the LORD your God in this way."

Israel's worship would gather instead of scatter. "You must seek the place the LORD your God will choose from among all your tribes to establish as a dwelling for His Name, and there you must go." To that one place they would bring the burnt offerings, the sacrifices, the tithes, the vowed gifts and the freewill gifts, the firstborn of herd and flock. And the gathering was not grim. "There, in the presence of the LORD your God, you and your households shall eat and rejoice in all you do, because the LORD your God has blessed you."

The Levite inside the gates was written into the rejoicing by name, the man with no portion or inheritance of his own. Twice in the chapter Moses stopped to say it again: rejoice, you and your sons and daughters and your servants, "and the Levite within your gates, since he has no portion or inheritance among you." And near the end, a warning shaped like a kindness: "Be careful not to neglect the Levites as long as you live in your land."

None of it could start yet. "You are not to do as we are doing here today, where everyone does what seems right in his own eyes." The camp still worshiped where it stood. "For you have not yet come to the resting place and the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you." The one altar waited on the far side of the Jordan, on the far side of the wars, in the rest he said God would give them from all the enemies around them.

Daily meat, though, would not need the journey. When a household craved meat, it could slaughter and eat within its own gates, clean and unclean together, the way a man eats a gazelle or a deer. One rule traveled home with the meat. "Only be sure not to eat the blood, because the blood is the life, and you must not eat the life with the meat." The blood was poured out on the ground like water. If the chosen place proved too far for the holy portions, those still went up: "But you are to take your holy things and your vow offerings and go to the place the LORD will choose."

Then Moses closed the chapter with the danger that comes after victory, and it was not an army. When the nations were cut off and Israel lived in their land, the temptation would be curiosity. "Do not inquire about their gods, asking," and here Moses put the question in their mouths before they could ask it: "How do these nations serve their gods? I will do likewise."

"You must not worship the LORD your God in this way". The reason was not that the old worship was weak or out of date. "They practice for their gods every abomination which the LORD hates. They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods." And over the whole chapter he set the seal he had set over the first address: "See that you do everything I command you; do not add to it or subtract from it."

Chapter 13 kept the same fight and moved it indoors. A prophet might arise, or a dreamer of dreams, and announce a sign or a wonder, and the sign might come true. Accuracy was not the test. If the voice behind the wonder said, "Let us follow other gods" and "let us worship them," Israel was not to listen. "For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul."

The answer to a working wonder was not a bigger wonder. It was a walk. "You are to follow the LORD your God and fear Him. Keep His commandments and listen to His voice; serve Him and hold fast to Him." The prophet himself was to die, Moses said, because he had advocated rebellion against the God who brought them out of Egypt, and the evil was to be purged from among them.

Then the test came closer than a prophet. It might come from "your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend", whispering in secret the same sentence: "Let us go and worship other gods". Moses did not soften what obedience would cost there. No yielding, no listening, no pity, no sparing, no shielding. The hand of the one enticed was to be first against him, and then the hands of all the people. "Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such a wicked thing among you."

The last case in the chapter was a whole city led astray by wicked men from among its own people, and here the law slowed down before it struck. A report was not enough. "Then you must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly." Only if the thing was established with certainty did the sword fall, on the people and the livestock together, and the city and all its plunder burned as a whole offering, left "a mound of ruins forever, never to be rebuilt." And a small, strange mercy was buried in the ashes: "Nothing devoted to destruction shall cling to your hands". No souvenirs from an apostate city. No profit from its fall.

Chapter 14 opened with a name before it gave a rule. "You are sons of the LORD your God". On the strength of that name, Israel was not to gash itself with the mourning cuts of its neighbors or shave the forehead for the dead, "for you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth."

The food list followed, the one Leviticus had already given, and Moses carried it the way it had been carried there, in a run: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer and the gazelle; anything with a split hoof that chews the cud; the camel, the rabbit, and the rock badger named as falling short of the rule; the pig, unclean; fish with fins and scales; the clean birds against the long roll of the unclean, eagle and vulture and owl and stork and bat; nothing that had died on its own on the table, though it could be given or sold to the foreigner inside the gates. And a kitchen rule with no reason attached, stated flat and left standing: "You must not cook a young goat in its mother's milk."

Then the chapter turned the tithe into a meal. A tenth of every year's produce was to be set aside and eaten by the family itself, at the chosen place, "so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always." And Moses had already met the objection forming in a farmer's mind, the one who lived too far away to carry what God had blessed him with. Convert it. "Then exchange it for money, take the money in your hand, and go to the place the LORD your God will choose." There, at the far end of the journey, the money turned back into a feast. "Then you may spend the money on anything you desire: cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink, or anything you wish. You are to feast there in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice with your household."

Every third year the tithe never left town. It was laid up inside the gates, and the guest list was the land's exposed people: "Then the Levite (because he has no portion or inheritance among you), the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied." The promise attached to it was not small: "And the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands."

Chapter 15 set the calendar underneath Israel's money. "At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts." Every creditor was to release what he had loaned to his neighbor, because the LORD's time of release had been proclaimed. A foreigner's debt could still be collected. A brother's could not. And Moses said the thing the release was built to make true: "There will be no poor among you". He tied it to the blessing on the land and to one condition, spoken in his own voice: "If only you obey the LORD your God and are careful to follow all these commandments I am giving you today." A people under that law, he said, would lend to many nations and borrow from none.

Then, in the same speech, he legislated for the poor man standing in the gate anyway. "If there is a poor man among your brothers within any of the gates in the land that the LORD your God is giving you, then you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother." The hand had its own instruction: "Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs."

Moses named the thought that would argue against the loan, and he named it wicked. As the seventh year approached, a lender's heart would do the arithmetic: "The seventh year, the year of release, is near". A debt about to be canceled is a gift wearing a loan's clothes, and the begrudging look that followed it would be answered in heaven: the poor brother would cry out to the LORD, and the guilt would land on the closed hand. So the command ran the other way. Give generously, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do. And then Moses set the two sentences of his own chapter side by side and harmonized neither of them: "For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land."

The seventh year released people as well as debts. A fellow Hebrew, man or woman, who had been sold into service served six years and went free in the seventh, and freedom was not to be an empty-handed push out the door. "You are to furnish him liberally from your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress. You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you." The reason underneath it was the one reason Deuteronomy never gets tired of: "Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today."

And the law left room for the servant who would not go. If he said he did not want to leave, because he loved the household and was well off in it, his ear was pierced with an awl against the door, and he stayed for life, his by choice. "Do not regard it as a hardship to set your servant free," Moses added to the masters, "because his six years of service were worth twice the wages of a hired hand."

The chapter closed where the chapters of settled life kept closing, at the altar and the table. Every firstborn male of herd and flock belonged to the LORD: not worked, not shorn, eaten year by year with the household at the chosen place. A blemished one, lame or blind, was never to be sacrificed, only eaten at home, clean and unclean together. And the blood, as always, was poured out on the ground like water.

Chapter 16 laid the year out as three journeys. The first came in the month of Abib, "because in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night." Passover was no longer a meal any town could hold on its own. "You are not to sacrifice the Passover animal in any of the towns that the LORD your God is giving you." It was offered only at the chosen place, in the evening as the sun set, at the same hour of day Israel had walked out of Egypt, and in the morning the families returned to their tents. With it, seven days of unleavened bread, and Moses gave the bread its name: "the bread of affliction, because you left the land of Egypt in haste". Its work was memory. Eat it, he said, "so that you may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt."

Seven weeks from the first swing of the sickle came the Feast of Weeks, its offering a freewill gift measured against the blessing each family had actually received. The rejoicing roll was read out again, sons and daughters, servants, the Levite, and the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you, and underneath the feast Moses set the same foundation stone: "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and carefully follow these statutes."

Last came Tabernacles, seven days after the threshing floor and the winepress had given up their produce, the harvest home and the year full. Moses promised the mood outright: "The LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that your joy will be complete."

Three times a year, then, the men of Israel were to appear before the LORD at the chosen place, at Unleavened Bread, at Weeks, at Tabernacles. "No one should appear before the LORD empty-handed." But the gift was scaled to the giver: "Everyone must appear with a gift as he is able, according to the blessing the LORD your God has given you." The poor man and the rich man climbed the same road. What they carried was measured by what they had been given.

And then, in the last breath of the section, Moses turned from altars and feasts to the men who would have to guard all of it. "You are to appoint judges and officials for your tribes in every town that the LORD your God is giving you. They are to judge the people with righteous judgment." No bending of justice, no partiality, and no bribes, "for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous." The sentence he left ringing over the courts was five words deep: "Pursue justice, and justice alone, so that you may live, and you may possess the land that the LORD your God is giving you."

One altar, one table kept clean, one calendar of feasts, one open hand. And beside the altar, a final small warning, easy to walk past: do not plant an Asherah pole next to it, and do not set up a sacred pillar, "which the LORD your God hates." What those judges would face, the cases too hard for a town gate, and the king Israel would one day ask for, were next in Moses' speech.

title: Judges, a King, and a Prophet to Come
subtitle: Deuteronomy 17 to 20, Berean Standard Bible
description: Courts are fenced with witnesses, the future king is placed under a book he must copy by hand, the prophet like Moses is promised, and refuge cities and the laws of war are set down.
paragraphs: The judges Moses had just appointed needed cases, courts, and limits, and the speech turned to all three. But chapter 17 began one step earlier, at the altar the judges would serve. "You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep with any defect or serious flaw, for that is detestable to the LORD your God." A settled people would be tempted to bring God the animal they could spare. The law closed that door first.

Then came the hardest case a town court would ever hear: a man or woman found worshiping other gods, bowing to the sun or the moon or the host of heaven. Moses built the procedure before he named the penalty, and the procedure slowed everything down. A report was not a verdict. "And if it is reported and you hear about it, you must investigate it thoroughly. If the report is true and such an abomination has happened in Israel," then the person was brought out to the gates and stoned.

Even then, one voice could not kill anyone. "On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death, but he shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness." And the witnesses carried the weight of their own words into their hands: "The hands of the witnesses shall be the first in putting him to death, and after that, the hands of all the people." A man who testified to a death had to start it. The chapter's refrain followed, the one this section of the speech keeps sounding: "So you must purge the evil from among you."

Some cases would be too hard for a town gate. Bloodshed, lawsuits, assaults, disputes the local judges could not settle were to go up to the one place, to the Levitical priests and to the judge presiding at that time. "Inquire of them, and they will give you a verdict in the case." The verdict from the chosen place was final. The people were to do everything instructed there, not turning aside "to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you".

The contempt that followed a refused verdict was itself a capital matter. "But the man who acts presumptuously, refusing to listen either to the priest who stands there to serve the LORD your God, or to the judge, must be put to death." Moses gave the reason the speech gives again and again for its hardest penalties: "Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly."

Then Moses did something stranger than sentencing. He legislated for a request nobody had made yet. "When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you and have taken possession of it and settled in it, and you say," and here the future request stands in the people's own words: "Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us". No king was commanded. No king was forbidden. The office was fenced before it existed.

The fences were these. The king would be the man "whom the LORD your God shall choose", taken from among their brothers, never a foreigner. And three appetites were capped before the first crown was ever cast. "But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses". Behind the horse trade stood the old road, and God's own sentence on it: "You are never to go back that way again." He must not take many wives, "lest his heart go astray". He must not accumulate large amounts of silver and gold.

The last fence was not a cap. It was a desk. "When he is seated on his royal throne, he must write for himself a copy of this instruction on a scroll in the presence of the Levitical priests." His own hand, his own copy, kept with him, read "all the days of his life". The purpose was stated plainly: "so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by carefully observing all the words of this instruction and these statutes". And the outcome Moses promised for a king under the book was not glory. "Then his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen". A king who read the law daily would reign as a brother among brothers, and he and his sons would reign many years in Israel.

Chapter 18 turned to the tribe with no desk and no land at all. The Levites held no portion or inheritance with Israel; the food offerings of the LORD were their inheritance, and Moses said it in the shortest form the speech uses for anything: "the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them". So the people's tables carried the priests. From every sacrifice, the shoulder, the jowls, and the stomach went to the priests. Firstfruits of grain, new wine, and oil, and the first wool off the flock, followed. And a Levite who left his own town and came in earnestness to the chosen place was to serve alongside his brothers there and "eat equal portions", even if he had money of his own from selling his father's estate. The tribe's poverty was structural, so the law made its support structural too.

From the priests Moses turned to the other voices the land would offer, and the list came down like a roll call: no one who "sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery," no one who "casts spells, consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead." This was not a list of superstitions to smile at. "For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD. And because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you." Israel was dispossessing peoples for these practices. To adopt them on arrival would be to move into a house and take up the crime it was emptied for. "You must be blameless before the LORD your God."

Against those voices Moses set the one voice God promised to keep sending. "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him." And he grounded the promise in the people's own request, the one from the day of the assembly at Horeb, when they had begged not to hear God's voice directly again. Their words stood in the text: "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!"

God's answer to that request was not rebuke. "They have spoken well." Then came the promise itself, in God's own words as Moses reported it: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him." And a weight hung on the listening: "And I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name."

The office had its own death penalty. A prophet who dared to speak in God's name what God had not commanded, or who spoke in the name of other gods, was to die. And Moses answered the question his hearers had not yet asked out loud. They might ask in their hearts: "How can we recognize a message that the LORD has not spoken?" The test was plain and unsparing: "When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken." The people owed such a man nothing, not even their fear. "Do not be afraid of him."

Chapter 19 went back to the ground, to cities and blood. When the nations were cut off and Israel settled in their cities and houses, three cities were to be set apart, with roads built to reach them and the land divided into three regions, so that a manslayer could flee and live. Moses told the case the cities existed for, and he told it as a work accident: two neighbors go into the forest to cut timber, the axe swings, "but the blade flies off the handle and strikes and kills his neighbor". No hatred, no intent, a tool failing in a man's hands. Without the city, the avenger of blood might pursue him in a rage and strike him dead on a long road, "though he did not deserve to die, since he did not intend any harm". If God enlarged the territory, three more cities were to be added, so that innocent blood would not be shed in the land.

The refuge had a wall the hater could not climb. "If, however, a man hates his neighbor and lies in wait, attacks him and kills him, and then flees to one of these cities," the elders of his own city were to send for him, bring him back, and hand him over to the avenger of blood to die. "You must show him no pity. You are to purge from Israel the guilt of shedding innocent blood, that it may go well with you." Mercy for the accidental, none for the ambush: the same chapter held both, and the difference was intent.

One sentence stood between the refuge cities and the witness laws, quiet enough to miss: "You must not move your neighbor's boundary marker, which was set up by your ancestors". In a land where the inheritance was the promise made visible, moving a stone in the night was theft against a man's grandchildren.

Then Moses returned to the courtroom, to the witness stand he had already built in chapter 17. A lone witness could never establish a charge, of any kind, against anyone. "A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses." But two witnesses could lie as well as one, so the law built a trap for the liar. Both parties were to stand before the LORD, before the priests and judges in office. "The judges shall investigate thoroughly, and if the witness is proven to be a liar who has falsely accused his brother," then the penalty the liar had aimed at his brother landed on the liar instead: "you must do to him as he intended to do to his brother".

Here, and only here in the speech, Moses laid down the measure in its famous form: "You must show no pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, and foot for foot." It stands in the text not as a license for revenge but as the sentence on a false witness, the punishment fitted exactly to the harm he tried to do by lying. And the refrain sounded over it a third time: the rest of the people would hear and be afraid, and never again do anything so evil among them.

Chapter 20 took the army out. "When you go out to war against your enemies and see horses, chariots, and an army larger than yours, do not be afraid of them; for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you." Before a blow was struck, the priest stepped forward with an address of his own: "Hear, O Israel, today you are going into battle with your enemies. Do not be fainthearted or afraid; do not be alarmed or terrified because of them. For the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory."

Then the officers shrank the army on purpose. "Has any man built a new house and not dedicated it? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man dedicate it." The same question went to the man who had planted a vineyard and not yet enjoyed its fruit, and to the man pledged to a woman and not yet married. Last, the officers asked the question no recruiting speech asks: "Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home, so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own." Only after the sendings-home did the officers appoint commanders and lead the army out. The ranks that marched were the ranks that remained after every man with an unfinished life, and every man whose fear might spread, had been sent back to his house.

When the army reached a city, the first weapon was an offer. "When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace." A city far away that opened its gates lived, and served. A city that refused war was besieged, and when God delivered it, its men fell and its spoil was taken. But the cities of the land itself, the inheritance, were another matter: "you must not leave alive anything that breathes." Moses gave the reason in the same breath, and it was the reason running under this whole section of the speech: "so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God."

The chapter's last law was aimed at the soldiers' own axes. In a long siege, the fruit trees around a city were not to be cut down for siege works, "because you can eat their fruit". Only trees that bore no food could be felled for the ramparts. And Moses left the army with a question that sounds almost like mercy reasoning with a siege line: "Are the trees of the field human, that you should besiege them?"

Courts, a king under a book, a tribe fed by the altar, a prophet still to come, cities of refuge with roads running to them, and an army that sends its fearful home. The machinery of a nation was on the table. What remained was smaller and harder: the cases waiting inside ordinary life, a lost ox, a found cloak, a wage unpaid at sundown. Moses turned to those next.

title: Life in the Land, Case by Case
subtitle: Deuteronomy 21 to 25, Berean Standard Bible
description: The covenant at the size of a household: an unsolved murder, a lost ox, a cloak returned by sunset, wages paid the same day, honest weights, and the memory of Amalek.
paragraphs: The speech now left the courts, the king, and the army behind and came down to the size of a field, a roof, a day's wage. Moses opened with a corpse.

"If one is found slain, lying in a field in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess, and it is not known who killed him," the elders and judges were to come out and measure. The town nearest the body took the case, whether it wanted it or not. Its elders brought a heifer that had never been yoked or worked to a valley with running water, ground never plowed or sown, and broke its neck there by the stream. The priests stood by. Then the elders washed their hands over the heifer and spoke their oath aloud: "Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it." And they prayed the prayer Moses gave them: "Accept this atonement, O LORD, for Your people Israel whom You have redeemed, and do not hold the shedding of innocent blood against them." An unsolved murder was not filed away. It was answered for, by the nearest town, in public, until the guilt of innocent blood was purged from the land.

The cases that followed ran the whole width of a life. A beautiful captive taken in war was to be given a full month in her captor's house to mourn her father and mother, her head shaved and her captivity clothes put aside, before she could become a wife. And if the man later lost his delight in her, he could not sell her or treat her as a slave. She went free, "since you have dishonored her."

Inheritance law protected the son nobody would have picked. A man with two wives, one beloved and one unloved, whose firstborn came from the unloved wife, could not hand the firstborn's double portion to the loved wife's son. "For that son is the firstfruits of his father's strength; the right of the firstborn belongs to him." A father's feelings did not rewrite a son's rights.

The hardest household case stood next. A stubborn and rebellious son, who would not obey his father and mother or listen when disciplined, was to be taken by both parents together to the elders at the gate. Their charge stands in the text: "This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard." Then all the men of the city stoned him, and the refrain of this section of the speech sounded for the fourth time: purge the evil from among you, and all Israel will hear and be afraid. And a body hung on a tree for a capital sin was never to hang overnight, "because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse". Bury him that day, Moses said, and do not defile the land.

Chapter 22 opened with a sentence Moses repeated until it sounded like a drumbeat: you must not ignore it. A brother's straying ox or sheep was to be brought home, not admired and left. If the owner was unknown or far away, the animal lived at the finder's house until its owner came looking, and the same held for a donkey, a cloak, "or anything your brother has lost and you have found." A donkey or ox fallen on the road was to be lifted, with its owner's help, not passed by. A lost animal, a fallen animal, a lost cloak: the law's eye kept landing on the moment a man decides his neighbor's trouble is not his business, and forbidding the decision.

Small laws followed, each with a world inside it. A woman was not to wear men's clothing, nor a man women's, for whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD. A bird's nest found along the road could be taken for its young or its eggs, but the mother was to be let go: "be sure to let the mother go, so that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days." Even a nest on the ground had an owner whose future the law guarded. A new house needed a railing around its roof, "so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls from it." The vineyard was not to be sown with two kinds of seed, nor an ox and a donkey yoked together, nor wool and linen woven into one garment, and tassels were to hang on the four corners of a man's cloak, the same tassels the wilderness generation had worn.

The rest of chapter 22 dealt with marriage and its violations, and Moses set the cases down plainly. A husband who slandered his bride's name, claiming she had not been a virgin, faced her parents and their proof before the elders; if the charge was a lie, he was punished, fined a hundred shekels of silver to her father, and kept the wife he had shamed, with no right to divorce her as long as he lived. If the charge was true, the woman died at her own father's door. A man found with another man's wife died, and so did the woman. The betrothed girl taken in the city, where a cry would have been heard, died with the man; the betrothed girl overpowered in the open country was guilty of nothing, for "the betrothed woman cried out, but there was no one to save her". Only the man died, her case weighed the same as a murder victim's. A virgin not pledged who was seized was to become the man's wife, her father paid fifty shekels, and that man too lost the right of divorce for life. No invention, no easing: the chapter graded harm by evidence, consent, and power, in a world with no police but the gate.

Chapter 23 drew the boundary of the assembly itself. Some were barred from it by birth or by injury, and Moab and Ammon were barred to the tenth generation, for a reason the story had already told: they met Israel on the road with no food and no water, and they hired Balaam to curse. But the exclusion carried its own memory inside it: "the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loves you." Edom, the brother nation, and Egypt, the old slave house, were treated more gently. "Do not despise an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land." By the third generation, their children could enter.

The war camp itself was to be kept holy, down to a spade in a soldier's kit and a place outside the camp, covered over, because "the LORD your God walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you". A slave who escaped to Israel was not to be handed back to his master; he was to live where he chose, unoppressed, in the town of his choosing. No son or daughter of Israel was to be a shrine prostitute, and no prostitute's wages could pay a vow in God's house. A brother was not to be charged interest on money, food, or anything lent. A vow once spoken was not to be slow in payment, though a vow never made carried no guilt at all. And a man walking through his neighbor's vineyard could eat his fill of grapes where he stood, so long as none went into his basket; in the grainfield he could pluck heads by hand, but the sickle stayed off his neighbor's grain.

Chapter 24 opened with the divorce case, and gave it in full legal dress: a man who finds some indecency in his wife writes her a certificate of divorce, hands it to her, and sends her from his house; if she remarries and that marriage ends by divorce or death, the first husband may never take her back, for that is an abomination to the LORD. Then the chapter turned, almost abruptly, to a wedding the law refused to interrupt. "If a man is newly married, he must not be sent to war or be pressed into any duty. For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married."

From there the cases tightened around the vulnerable. A millstone could not be taken as security for a debt, "because that would be taking one's livelihood as security." A man caught kidnapping an Israelite brother, to enslave or sell him, was to die. Skin diseases were to be handled exactly as the priests instructed, and Miriam's name was set down as the reminder of what pride cost on the road. A lender was not to walk into a borrower's house to seize the pledge; he stood outside, and the borrower brought it out. If the pledge was a poor man's cloak, it went back before sunset regardless of the debt: "be sure to return it to him by sunset, so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you". And the lender's restraint, not his generosity, was what heaven counted: this, Moses said, "will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God".

Then came the wage law, among the most practical sentences in the whole speech. "Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy, whether he is a brother or a foreigner residing in one of your towns. You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them." A day laborer has no reserves; his wage that night is his supper. Hold it back, Moses warned, "he may cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin."

Justice between generations was cut clean: "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin." No justice was to be denied the foreigner or the fatherless, no widow's cloak taken as a pledge, and under both rulings ran the reason this book never lets go of: "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place."

The chapter closed in the harvest field. A sheaf forgotten in the field was not to be fetched back. The olives were beaten once, not gone over a second time; the vines were picked once, not stripped clean. What remained belonged to "the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow," and the blessing promised for leaving it was the blessing on all the work of a man's hands. The law built its poor relief into the harvest itself: the margin of every field was, by statute, somebody else's supper.

Chapter 25 set the limits of the rod. A guilty man flogged in the judge's presence could receive no more than forty lashes, "lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight." Even a condemned man stayed a brother. And an ox treading grain was not to be muzzled: the worker, animal or man, ate from the work under his feet.

Then the levirate case. When brothers lived together and one died without a son, his widow was not to marry outside the family; the surviving brother was to take her, and "the first son she bears will carry on the name of the dead brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel." A man could refuse. But the refusal was public: the widow told the elders her charge, "My husband's brother refuses to preserve his brother's name in Israel", the elders reasoned with him, and if he held to his refusal he stood barefoot before them while she removed his sandal and spat in his face, with the sentence spoken over him: "This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother's line." His family's name in Israel, from that day, was "The House of the Unsandaled." A name kept for a dead brother was worth more to the law than a living man's pride. In a fight, a wife who rescued her husband by seizing his opponent's genitals lost her hand for it, with no pity shown; the law guarded even a brawler's body in the moment of the grapple.

The last laws of the section reached into a merchant's bag. "You shall not have two differing weights in your bag, one heavy and one light." Not two measures in the house, one large and one small, a big one for selling and a small one for buying. "You must maintain accurate and honest weights and measures, so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you." Fraud at the scales was not sharp practice. "For everyone who behaves dishonestly in regard to these things is detestable to the LORD your God."

And the speech's long case list ended where Deuteronomy keeps ending, in memory. "Remember what the Amalekites did to you along your way from Egypt". Moses had not forgotten the first enemy Israel ever faced, the raiders who fell on the march at its weakest point: "how they met you on your journey when you were tired and weary, and they attacked all your stragglers; they had no fear of God." The weak at the back of the column, cut down by men who feared nothing. So when God gave Israel rest from the enemies around them in the land, one sentence stood waiting to be carried out: "you are to blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Do not forget!"

A heifer by a stream for a killer nobody caught. A railing on a roof. A cloak returned by sunset. A wage paid before the sun went down. A sheaf left standing in the corner of a field. The cases were the covenant at the size of a household, and they rested, nearly all of them, on one sentence Moses had said so many times his hearers could say it with him: you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you. What came next was the part of the speech no one could file under daily life at all: firstfruits carried to the altar, two mountains facing each other across a valley, and a choice that would be read aloud to a nation.

title: Firstfruits, Two Mountains, and the Choice Set Down
subtitle: Deuteronomy 26 to 29, Berean Standard Bible
description: A farmer recites the whole story over a basket of firstfruits, two mountains answer Amen to the curses, blessings and curses are set in full, and the covenant is renewed in Moab.
paragraphs: The long list of cases closed, and Moses turned from laws to ceremonies, from what Israel must do every day to what Israel must say out loud. Chapter 26 gave every farmer a speech.

"When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, and you take possession of it and settle in it," the first produce of the soil was to go into a basket and up to the chosen place. The farmer handed it to the priest with a one-line declaration: "I declare today to the LORD your God that I have entered the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us." Then, with the basket set before the altar, he recited the whole story of his people in one paragraph, and Moses made every Israelite memorize the words generations before any of them farmed an acre.

"My father was a wandering Aramean, and he went down to Egypt few in number and lived there and became a great nation, mighty and numerous. But the Egyptians mistreated us and afflicted us, putting us to hard labor. So we called out to the LORD, the God of our fathers; and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, toil, and oppression. Then the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, signs, and wonders. And He brought us to this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey. And now, behold, I have brought the firstfruits of the land that You, O LORD, have given me."

Jacob the wanderer, Egypt the furnace, the cry, the mighty hand, the land. A creed a man could say in under a minute, standing over his own harvest, tying his basket to Abraham. Then he bowed, and the rejoicing that followed the confession had its usual guest list written in: the farmer, the Levite, and the foreigner dwelling among them, rejoicing together "in all the good things the LORD your God has given to you and your household". History first, then gratitude, then the table shared.

The third year brought the second declaration, the tithe year, when the tenth stayed in the towns for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The farmer who had given it stood before God and audited himself aloud: "I have removed from my house the sacred portion and have given it to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all the commandments You have given me. I have not transgressed or forgotten Your commandments." Nothing eaten in mourning, nothing handled while unclean, nothing offered to the dead. And the declaration ended as a prayer: "Look down from Your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless Your people Israel and the land You have given us as You swore to our fathers".

Then Moses closed the chapter with an exchange of proclamations, the covenant spoken in both directions on the same day. "Today you have proclaimed that the LORD is your God and that you will walk in His ways, keep His statutes and commandments and ordinances, and listen to His voice. And today the LORD has proclaimed that you are His people and treasured possession as He promised". The promise attached to it was elevation: God would set Israel "high in praise and name and honor above all the nations He has made," a holy people, "as He has promised."

Chapter 27 moved the ceremony to the far side of the Jordan. "On the day you cross the Jordan into the land that the LORD your God is giving you," large stones were to be set up on Mount Ebal, coated with plaster, and written over with all the words of this law. Beside them, an altar, and the altar had a rule the stones did not: "You must not use any iron tool on them." Uncut stones only. On that altar, burnt offerings, and peace offerings eaten there in rejoicing, and the law on the plastered stones written, Moses insisted, distinctly, where a whole nation could read what it had agreed to. Then Moses and the priests called the camp to attention with a sentence that measured the day: "Be silent, O Israel, and listen! This day you have become the people of the LORD your God."

The tribes were then divided between two facing mountains. On Mount Gerizim, to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. On Mount Ebal, to deliver the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali. Between them, the Levites were to proclaim the curses in a loud voice, and to every curse the whole people answered with one word: "Amen!"

The twelve curses ran like a roll of hidden sins dragged into the open. "Cursed is the man who makes a carved idol or molten image" and "sets it up in secret." Cursed, the man who dishonors his father or mother. Cursed, the man who moves his neighbor's boundary stone, the theft Moses had already forbidden in a whisper of a verse. Cursed, the man who lets a blind man wander in the road. Cursed, the man who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow. Then the curses from the forbidden beds, the father's wife, the animal, the sister, the mother-in-law. Cursed, the man who strikes down his neighbor in secret, and the man who accepts a bribe to kill an innocent person. Secret is the word that keeps returning: sins no court could catch, named aloud on a mountainside, with the entire nation answering for them. And the last curse covered all the rest: "Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice." Amen, said everyone.

Chapter 28 then set the two futures down in full, and Moses built them as mirrors. The blessings came first, fourteen verses of abundance chasing a man down. "And all these blessings will come upon you and overtake you, if you will obey the voice of the LORD your God". Blessed in the city and blessed in the country. The fruit of the womb blessed, the produce of the land, the calves and the lambs. "Your basket and kneading bowl will be blessed. You will be blessed when you come in and blessed when you go out." Enemies would march out in one direction and flee in seven. God would decree blessing on the barns and on everything the hand touched, open the heavens, His storehouse, with rain in season, and make Israel "the head and not the tail", a lender to many nations that borrowed from none.

Then the mirror turned.
